title: Words Into Numbers

post.author: u/cribsheet_cosima
post.title: My great-aunt left me her codebreaker's attic and a notebook that turns words into numbers. It reads every message she ever wrote. It can't read her name.

blocks.text: Great-aunt Ysolde died in March and left me her attic: four filing cabinets of index cards, a typewriter, and a green notebook with BOOK OF PAIRS on the cover. She worked with codes all her life and never once said for whom.

Every card holds a message in Dutch, as it came in, with her English translation typed underneath. She typed English like a telegram: no capitals, no commas, and the word *stop* for a full stop. She signed each card in ink: Ysolde Vranckx.

The notebook is a numbered list. Entries 0 to 36 are the space, the ten digits and the 26 letters. Inside the front cover she copied twelve of her English messages. Entry 37 is t and h, joined, with 30 in pencil beside it: she had counted every pair of neighbouring symbols inside each word, a space joining the word after it and never the word before, and t then h was the commonest. She gave the pair its own number, rewrote the messages with it, and counted again. Entry 38 is 37 and e. She did that 63 times. The book stops at entry 99.

I'm a junior developer, so last night I typed her rules into a small program that does what she did by hand: split a line into single symbols, then make her joins in order, 37 to 99. Her words come out whole. *stop* is one number. *courier* is one number. Then I tried card 1 from the top drawer, which isn't among the twelve.

english  the courier waits at the bridge at dawn stop
         9 words   44 characters   13 numbers
dutch    de koerier wacht bij zonsopgang bij de brug stop
         9 words   48 characters   37 numbers
signed   ysolde vranckx
         2 words   14 characters   14 numbers

Same card, same nine words, and the Dutch takes nearly three times as many numbers. Her own name comes apart into one number per character, the space included. Times too: 0400, which she wrote three times in the twelve, is one number. 0340 is four.
It knows every word she wrote. It doesn't know her.

Here's why I'm asking. I'm about to pay a language model to translate all 2,400 cards, one card per request with my instructions on top. It charges by the token, so much per million. Its help page gives a rule of thumb, about three quarters of a word per token, and has a token counter you can paste text into. I used the rule and budgeted from the word count.
Is the model's reader built anything like her book? And what are those 2,400 cards really going to cost?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Sorry about your great-aunt. Nothing in that notebook is haunted. She built what engineers call a tokenizer. It cuts text into tokens, pieces that can be a whole word, part of a word or one character, and swaps each for its token id, its number in a fixed list called the vocabulary. Each join is a merge, and building the list by merging the commonest pair again and again is called byte-pair encoding. Language models read ids, never letters, and their tokenizers were built the same way from their own piles of text. Providers run two meters: input tokens, everything you send, and output tokens, everything the model writes back, each priced per million. So, two questions. Whose writing did she count pairs in? And which of those meters did your word count measure?

replies.author: u/cribsheet_cosima
replies.text: Only her own English. Twelve messages, copied inside the front cover. Not one word of Dutch. And I counted the words on the Dutch side of the cards, nothing else.

comments.author: u/subtitle_desk_tove
comments.text: I do subtitles for a small streaming service, in five languages. We pay an AI service by the token to draft them, and the same episode costs us more in some of our languages than in others. Same episode, same scenes, same running time. It took me a month to believe the invoices.

comments.author: u/pencil_cipher_ilka
comments.text: Counting neighbouring pairs is the first thing my cipher club does with a new puzzle. In a substitution cipher, where every letter is swapped for another, the commonest pairs give the game away. Your aunt turned the trick inside out. She wasn't counting pairs to break a code. She was counting them to build one.

replies.author: u/cribsheet_cosima
replies.text: Under entry 99, in the same pencil, the book has one more line: whatever is not in here, it spells. I read the twelve messages again tonight. Her name isn't in them. Neither is mine.

reply.prompt: The cards are boxed by the stairs and the budget is set. What should Cosima do before she sends the first card? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the word-count budget. The provider's rule of thumb, about three quarters of a word per token, was worked out on huge amounts of text, so over 2,400 cards it will average out.
options.verdict: A rule for English, used on Dutch
options.part2: I sent cards all Friday night. By card 400 I had used most of the money set aside for all 2,400. The rule of thumb is written for English, and almost everything I sent was Dutch, with her name and a card number on every one, and my instructions went out again with every single card. I'd also forgotten that the English coming back is billed too, at the higher output price. I stopped there and did the sum again, properly.
options.senior: The rule of thumb is for English text, and the provider labels it that way. Other languages, names, numbers and code often take more tokens per word, instructions are sent with every request, and the reply is billed as output. Estimate from real counts, not words.

options.text: Put her method to work: train my own tokenizer on the Dutch cards so most Dutch words become one token, then send the model my token ids instead of the text, and pay for far fewer.
options.verdict: The model only knows its own ids
options.part2: I trained a tokenizer on 300 Dutch cards and sent the model my ids, written out as text, since text is all it takes. Its own tokenizer read them as digits and spaces, more tokens than the Dutch had been. Then it answered, politely, that the message appeared to be a numeric code, and asked whether I had the key. I laughed until I remembered whose attic I was sitting in.
options.senior: A model only knows what the ids of its own vocabulary mean, because it was trained on them. On a hosted model you choose the text you send, not the tokenizer, so measure the tokens of the model you will actually use.

options.text: Before sending anything, take cards from every cabinet, with my instructions attached, and count them with the provider's token counter. Price input and output tokens separately, then scale up.
options.part2: I took 25 cards from each cabinet, 100 in all, put my instructions on each, and ran them through the provider's token counter. The instructions were a bigger share of every request than I'd guessed, so I cut them to four lines. I translated ten cards for real, read the output token counts the service reported, priced input and output separately, scaled to 2,400 and added a fifth for luck. The bill came in under it. Her book still reads card 1 as 13 tokens in English and 37 in Dutch. The real counter was kinder to the Dutch than her book. It was never kind to her name.
options.senior: Count, don't guess: a sample that looks like the real job, counted with the provider's own counter for the model you'll use, input and output priced separately, then a margin. After launch, check the usage the service reports against the estimate.

options.text: Switch to the cheapest model the provider has that reads Dutch. Its price per million tokens is a fifth of the one I picked, so even if the cards take more tokens, the bill will shrink.
options.verdict: Trade-off: cheaper, but nowhere near a fifth
options.part2: The bill did come in lower, but nowhere near a fifth: the cheap model split the Dutch into more tokens than the first one and wrote longer translations. It also spelled Vranckx three different ways and twice turned a card number into a date. My cousins found the mistakes before I did.
options.senior: Cost per card is tokens times price, and the same text can split into a different number of tokens on a different model. A cheaper model can be the right choice, but only after you count its tokens and check its quality on the same sample.

sim.title: Build her book yourself
sim.lede: You're Cosima in the attic, a quarter past midnight, with Ysolde's Book of Pairs open. The tokenizer here learns the way she did, from her twelve English messages, shown at the bottom: start from the 37 symbols (the space, ten digits and 26 letters), count every pair of neighbouring symbols, merge the commonest into a new token, and repeat. A tie goes to the pair that appears first in her messages. The slider sets how many merges to use, from 0 to her 63, and so the vocabulary size, from 37 to 100. Pick a line from the story; each chip is one token with its token id, the middle dot is a space glued to the front of a token, and amber chips are single characters. The two costs use made-up teaching prices, not any provider's: $6 per million input tokens and $24 per million output tokens, for a million copies of the line, so each cost is the tokens times the price.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start with all 63 merges on card 1's English: 13 tokens for 44 characters, 3.4 characters per token, $78 to send a million copies as input. Slide to 0: every character is its own token, 44 of them. Slide up slowly and watch stop become one token at 6 merges and courier at 30, while the merge list grows. Now pick the Dutch: 37 tokens at 63 merges, for the same nine words. Pick her signature: 14 tokens at every setting, because none of its pairs is ever merged. Compare the two times, 0400 and 0340. Last, press Count all five lines, and check the cost math in the note under the chips: tokens times $6 for input, times $24 for output.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the notebook is haunted. Ysolde built a tokenizer: she merged the commonest pairs of symbols in her own English, so her words come out whole, while Dutch, a time she never wrote and a name missing from her twelve messages fall apart into letters. A language model's bill is counted in those pieces.

steps.title: A model reads numbers, not letters.
steps.text: A language model can't read letters. Before it sees anything, a tokenizer cuts the text into tokens, pieces that are often a whole word, sometimes part of one, sometimes a single character, and swaps each for its token id, its row number in a fixed list called the vocabulary. Ysolde's book is a tiny tokenizer with a vocabulary of 100. Card 1's English becomes 13 ids: 38 66 61 29 50 43 70 50 87 11 33 24 42. The model reads those ids, and when it answers it writes ids too, which the tokenizer turns back into text. Nothing is lost on the way: looking each id up and joining the pieces gives back the exact text, spaces included. OpenAI's tiktoken lists the same property: reversible and lossless.

steps.title: How her book was built: byte-pair encoding.
steps.text: Her method has a name. Byte-pair encoding began as a compression technique that replaces the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte. In 2016, Sennrich, Haddow and Birch adapted it to split words for machine translation. Start with single characters. Count every pair of neighbouring symbols in a training text, merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and repeat. Each merge adds one entry, so the vocabulary is the starting symbols plus the merges: her 37 plus 63 make 100. The number of merges is the one setting you choose. Ties need a rule so the result never changes: in the sim, the pair that appears first in the text wins. To read new text, the tokenizer splits it into characters and replays the merges in the order they were learned. Sennrich's version never merges across a word boundary, and neither does her book. Her book has one more habit worth knowing: a space belongs to the word after it, so the same word gets a different id at the start of a line and in mid-sentence: *the* at the start of a line is entry 38, and *the* with a space in front is entry 43.

steps.title: Why her words come out whole and her name doesn't.
steps.text: A merge only exists if its pair was common in the training text. Her twelve messages say *stop* 19 times and *courier* three times, so both became single tokens. *Dawn* isn't in the twelve, so card 1 spells it out: a space and *d*, then *a*, *w*, *n*. Her name isn't in them either, and not one of its pairs was ever merged, so it stays one token per character however many merges you allow. The Dutch is the same message as the English, nine words each, but her book was built from English only, so most Dutch pairs were never merged: 37 tokens against 13. Numbers split by habit, not by value: 0400, which she wrote three times, is one token, and 0340 is four. Real tokenizers learn from far more text and have far bigger vocabularies, so they split much less than her book. The pattern is the same, though: rare names, typos, unusual numbers, code and languages that were scarce in the tokenizer's training text break into more pieces. Among 100 rare words in their German training data, Sennrich's team found 56 compounds and 21 names.

steps.title: Tokens are what you pay for, and what limits you.
steps.text: Providers bill per token, on two meters: input tokens, everything you send (instructions, the card, any examples), and output tokens, everything the model writes back. Each has its own price per million tokens, and the output price is usually the higher one. The cost of a request is tokens times price, divided by 1,000,000, once for input and once for output. Anthropic's pricing page works one through: 50,000 input tokens times $5, divided by 1,000,000, is $0.25. Limits are counted in tokens too, such as how much a model can read at once, its context window, which case 5 covers. A word count only guesses at tokens. OpenAI's rule of thumb, about 4 characters or three quarters of a word per token, is labelled as a rule for English, and the same page says other languages can have different relationships between characters, words and tokens. And different models can have different tokenizers, so the same text can have different counts.

steps.title: Next: each id becomes a list of numbers.
steps.text: A token id is only a row number. 66 says nothing about couriers, and it is no more like 65 than like 3. Inside the model, each id picks out a row of learned numbers, a vector called an embedding, and that is where meaning starts. The next case opens that table.

diagram.aria: What happens to card 1 on its way through a language model. Card 1's English, 9 words and 44 characters, is split into 13 tokens such as the, courier, wait and s. The tokens are looked up as 13 token ids, starting 38 66 61 29, the input tokens, billed at the input price per million. The language model reads only ids and writes ids back: the output ids, written one at a time, are the output tokens, billed at the output price, which is often several times higher. The output ids are looked up and joined back into English text.

notes.text: billed at the input price, per million
billed at the output price, often higher
cost = tokens x price per million / 1,000,000

explain.caption: Read clockwise from the top left. The tokenizer splits card 1's English into 13 tokens and looks up their ids. Those 13 ids are the input tokens. The model reads only ids and writes ids back, one at a time, and those are the output tokens, priced separately. Each meter costs tokens times its price per million, divided by 1,000,000.

fix.title: The fix: count tokens, don't guess them
fix.text: Budget from real token counts, not words. Take a sample that looks like the real job: cards from every cabinet, in both languages, with the names and numbers, and with the instructions you'll send every time, because they are input tokens on every request. Count it with the provider's own token counter for the exact model you will use. Anthropic's counting endpoint, for example, is free to call within its rate limits. Estimate the output separately: run a few real requests and read the output token counts the service reports, and set a limit on answer length where the service offers one. Multiply each meter by its price per million, add a margin, and scale up to the whole job. After launch, compare the bill with the usage the service reports, and count again whenever you change models.

limits: A counter only measures the text you already have. Output tokens don't exist until the model writes them, so the output side of any estimate is a forecast from samples, and changing the instructions can move it.

Counts belong to one model. Anthropic calls its count an estimate that can differ by a small amount from the tokens actually used, and says its newer tokenizer produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text than its earlier models did, so a count from one model can't be reused for another.
A sample misleads like any small sample. If all 100 cards come from one cabinet, the estimate inherits that cabinet's languages and lengths. Draw it from everywhere the real work will come from.

head: What matters
Small vocabulary (few merges)
Large vocabulary (many merges)
rows: Many. With no merges, one per character: card 1's English is 44.
Fewer. Common words become one token each: card 1 is 13 with all 63 merges.
Spelled out in tiny pieces, but never unreadable.
Still split if they were rare in the training text, though into bigger pieces.
Small: few ids, each seen often in training.
Large: every id needs its own learned row, and rare ones get little practice.
More tokens per message, so each one costs more and less fits at once.
Fewer tokens per message, so each one costs less and more fits.
The model's builders, before training. You can't change it on a hosted model.
The same. You choose the model, not its tokenizer.

explain.seniorTake: Treat tokens as the unit of cost and limits, and budget from token counts rather than words. Count with the provider's own counter, for the model you will use, on a sample that looks like the real traffic with the instructions included, and price input and output separately. A rule of thumb is a first guess for English. For other languages, names, numbers or code, measure.

realWorld.title: Byte-pair encoding, from compression to translation
realWorld.text: In 2016, Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch at the University of Edinburgh adapted byte-pair encoding, a simple compression technique that replaces the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte, to split words into subword units for neural machine translation. Their version starts each word as a sequence of characters, counts all symbol pairs, and replaces each occurrence of the most frequent pair with a new symbol. The final vocabulary size is the starting vocabulary plus the number of merges, and that number is the algorithm's only hyperparameter, the one setting chosen before training. It never merges across word boundaries. Their motivation was rare words: among 100 rare words in their German training data they found 56 compounds and 21 names. Subword units let a model with a fixed vocabulary translate and even produce words it never saw in training.

realWorld.title: tiktoken, OpenAI's tokenizer
realWorld.text: OpenAI describes tiktoken as a fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI's models, and lists what byte-pair encoding gives: it is reversible and lossless, so tokens convert back into the original text; it works on arbitrary text, even text that wasn't in the tokenizer's training data; and it compresses, so that on average, in practice, each token corresponds to about 4 bytes. It also lets the model see common subwords: its example splits *encoding* into *encod* and *ing*.

realWorld.title: OpenAI's rule of thumb, and where it stops
realWorld.text: OpenAI's help page on tokens gives rough estimates under the heading Use rough estimates for English text: 1 token is approximately 4 characters, or three-quarters of a word, and 100 tokens are approximately 75 words. It says these are estimates, not exact counts, that other languages can have different relationships between characters, words, and tokens, and that the same text can produce different token counts depending on the model, its encoding, and the language. It tracks input and output tokens separately, and they can have different prices.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: priced per million, counted per model
realWorld.text: Anthropic prices Claude models per million tokens, written MTok, with separate prices for input and output tokens. When this case was written, every model on its pricing page had an output price five times its input price. Its worked example: 50,000 input tokens times $5, divided by 1,000,000, is $0.25, and 15,000 output tokens times $25, divided by 1,000,000, is $0.375. Its token counting endpoint counts a message's input tokens before you send it, is free to use within rate limits, and returns what the docs call an estimate. The docs also say that Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30 percent more tokens for the same text, depending on the content, and tell developers to recount prompts against the model they plan to use instead of reusing older counts.

realWorld.title: The same text, up to 15 times the tokens
realWorld.text: At NeurIPS 2023, Aleksandar Petrov, Emanuele La Malfa, Philip Torr and Adel Bibi showed that the same text translated into different languages can have drastically different tokenization lengths, with differences up to 15 times in some cases, and that the gaps persist even for tokenizers trained on purpose to support many languages. Character-level and byte-level models showed over 4 times the difference for some language pairs. They spell out what that means for people: some language communities pay more for the same commercial service, wait longer for it, and can give the model less context.

asked: Why can the same text cost more on one model than on another, or in one language than in another?
Estimate the monthly token cost of a feature that answers 20,000 customer questions a day.
interview.answer: Cost is tokens times price, and both parts move. Tokens depend on the tokenizer: each model family learned its own vocabulary from its own training text, so the same sentence splits differently, and Anthropic's docs give a real case, a newer tokenizer that produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text. Languages that were scarce in a tokenizer's training text split into more pieces: Petrov and colleagues found up to 15 times the tokens for the same text. Price per token differs by model too, and output usually costs more than input. For the estimate, say each assumption out loud and then measure it: requests (20,000 a day, about 600,000 a month), input tokens per request (the instructions, the question and anything looked up, counted with the provider's counter on real samples, say 1,500), and output tokens per request (from sample runs, say 300). At teaching prices of $6 per million input tokens and $24 per million output tokens: 600,000 times 1,500 is 900 million input tokens, $5,400; 600,000 times 300 is 180 million output tokens, $4,320; about $9,720 a month. Then name the levers: shorter instructions, less looked-up text, shorter answers, a cheaper model where quality holds, and a check of the real bill against the estimate in the first week.

terms.def: A piece of text that a language model reads or writes: often a whole word with its leading space, sometimes part of a word, sometimes one character. Costs and limits are counted in tokens.
A token's number in the vocabulary. The model sees only these numbers. In Ysolde's book, the word *the* with a space in front is 43.
The program that cuts text into tokens and turns them into token ids, and turns ids back into text. Each model comes with its own.
Cutting text into tokens. Different tokenizers cut the same text differently.
The fixed, numbered list of every token a tokenizer knows. Ysolde's has 100 entries; real ones have tens of thousands or more.
How many entries the vocabulary has. In byte-pair encoding it is the starting symbols plus the number of merges: 37 plus 63 is 100.
A piece of a word, like ing or a single letter. Rare words are written as several subwords instead of being unknown.

A way to build a vocabulary: start from single characters or bytes, merge the most frequent pair of neighbouring symbols into a new one, and repeat until the vocabulary is the size you want. Also called BPE.
Short for byte-pair encoding.
One step of byte-pair encoding: two neighbouring symbols joined into a new vocabulary entry, like t and h into th. Ysolde called them joins.
For a tokenizer, the text its merges are learned from. Ysolde's is twelve English messages. What is common there comes out whole; what is rare stays in pieces.
One letter, digit, space or other single symbol of text.
The basic unit computers store text in. An English letter takes one byte; letters of many other scripts take two to four.
Nothing is lost on the round trip: turning the tokens back into text gives exactly the text you started with.
Every token you send a model on a request: instructions, examples, the user's text. Billed at the input price.
Every token the model writes back. Billed at the output price, which is usually higher than the input price.
How providers quote prices: dollars for every million tokens, separately for input and output. Cost is tokens times price, divided by 1,000,000.
Anthropic's short form for a million tokens. $5 / MTok means $5 for every million tokens.
A tool from the provider that counts how many tokens a text will be for a given model, before you send it.
A rough guide for a first estimate, like a token being about three quarters of an English word. It is not a measurement.
A made-up price used in this case's sim and interview answer to show the arithmetic. It is not any provider's real price.
One message sent to a model's service, and the one answer that comes back.
A company that runs language models and sells access to them, billed by the token.
A model a provider runs for you. You send text and get text back; you can't change its tokenizer or its training.
Application programming interface: the way one program asks another for something, like sending a model a request and getting its answer.
One address in an API that does one job, like counting the tokens of a message.
A cap on how many requests you may send in a period of time, like requests per minute.
The most tokens a model can take in at once, counting what you send and, for many models, what it writes. Case 5 of this season covers it.
A list of numbers. Inside a model, each token id picks out one.
The vector of learned numbers a model keeps for each token id, its row in a big table. The next case is about embeddings.
A setting chosen before training rather than learned, like the number of merges in byte-pair encoding.
Storing the same information in less space, for example by replacing a common pair of symbols with one new symbol.
Translating text from one language to another with a program. Neural machine translation uses a neural network to do it.
A word built from other words, like the German Sonnensystem, solar system. Many rare words are compounds.
OpenAI's open-source byte-pair encoding tokenizer for its models.
An AI company that makes the Claude models and publishes their prices and token counting docs.
Anthropic's family of language models.
Neural Information Processing Systems, one of the main yearly research conferences in machine learning.
Someone who reads coded messages without being given the key.
A way of hiding a message by changing its letters by a rule, so only someone with the key can read it.
A cipher that swaps every letter for another letter. Counting which letters and pairs are common is the classic way to break one.
A small stiff card for one record, kept in order in a drawer or filing cabinet.
A short message sent by wire and paid for by length, so it was written with no spare words. The word stop stood in for a full stop.
The text of what is said in a film or show, shown on screen, often translated into other languages.

atWork: Pick one feature at work that calls a language model, or the one you'd most like to build. Find what it sends on every request: the instructions, any examples, any documents it pastes in, and the user's text. Count each part with the provider's token counter for the model it really uses, and read the output token counts the service reports for a few real requests. Multiply each meter by its price per million and by a month of traffic. Then count again with a message in each language your users write in, and with long names, order numbers or code if they turn up. If the instructions are the biggest part of every request, or one language costs far more than another, you've found where the bill comes from before the bill finds you.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant answers customers in English, and its bill has been steady for months. Next quarter it opens to customers who write in Thai and Polish, with the same traffic. Your manager budgets the same amount per conversation. What do you tell them, and what do you check first?

keyIdeas.idea: Other languages often split into more tokens for the same meaning, so the same conversation can cost more
Measure with the provider's token counter on real samples in each new language
Input and output are priced separately, and the replies in those languages are billed too
Count for the exact model in use, and watch the real usage after it opens

recall.model: I'd tell them the budget is a guess until we measure, because cost is counted in tokens, not conversations, and other languages often split into more tokens for the same meaning. Before it opens, I'd collect real sample conversations in Thai and Polish, count them with the provider's token counter for the exact model we use, and price input and output separately, since the replies in those languages are billed too. If the counts per conversation are higher than for English, the budget goes up by that much. After launch I'd watch the usage the service reports per language and compare it with the estimate.

recall.prompt: In Ysolde's book, card 1's English took 13 tokens and the Dutch on the same card took 37, though both are nine words. Why?
options: Dutch words are longer, and a tokenizer always gives one token per character
The tokenizer drops letters it doesn't know, then pads the line back out
Dutch needs more tokens in every tokenizer, because of how the language works
Her book was built from English messages only, so few Dutch pairs were merged
recall.why: A merge only exists if its pair was common in the training text, and hers was twelve English messages. Dutch pairs were rarely merged, so the Dutch stays in small pieces. A tokenizer trained on plenty of Dutch would split it far less.

recall.prompt: Explain byte-pair encoding to a new teammate: how the vocabulary is built, how a new word gets cut up, and why a rare surname ends up as several pieces.

keyIdeas.idea: Start from single characters or bytes
Repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new entry, until the vocabulary reaches a chosen size
New text starts as characters, then the learned merges are replayed in order
A rare word's pairs were seldom merged, so it stays in small pieces

recall.model: You start with the single characters, or bytes, as the vocabulary. Then you count every pair of neighbouring symbols in a big training text, merge the most frequent pair into a new entry, rewrite the text with it, and repeat until the vocabulary is the size you chose. To read a new word, you start from its characters and replay the learned merges in the order they were learned. Common words end up as one token. A rare surname's pairs were seldom or never merged, because they hardly appeared in the training text, so it stays in several small pieces.

recall.prompt: At teaching prices of $6 per million input tokens and $24 per million output tokens, a request sends 2,000 tokens and gets 500 back. What does it cost?
recall.why: Each meter is tokens times price, divided by 1,000,000: input 2,000 times $6 is $0.012, output 500 times $24 is $0.012, so $0.024 in all. $0.015 prices everything at the input rate, $0.06 everything at the output rate, and $0.051 swaps the two prices.

recall.prompt: Why can't you send a hosted model the ids from a tokenizer you trained yourself, to save tokens?
options: You can, as long as the ids are sent as numbers instead of as text
Its tokenizer is a setting you can switch on each request
It only learned what its own vocabulary's ids mean, during training
Its token counter would reject the request before it arrived
recall.why: A model's training ties it to one tokenizer: it learned what each of its own ids means. Your ids would mean nothing to it, and sent as text they are just digits for its own tokenizer to cut up, often into more tokens than the words.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. All 2,400 cards are translated, and my budget held. My cousin Ottavio liked it so much that his family-history website now offers the same thing: upload an old letter, get it back in English. He priced it from my numbers, the average card in tokens times his price per million. In the first month the uploads came from everywhere: letters in Greek, Polish and Vietnamese, old handwriting typed up by users, long lists of names and dates. He also sends a full page of instructions with each upload. The bill was more than twice his estimate.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why was Ottavio's estimate wrong, and how should he budget a feature like this?

keyIdeas.idea: He estimated from Cosima's cards, which don't look like his users' letters: other languages, names and numbers split into more tokens
The page of instructions is input on every request, and the translations coming back are billed as output
Measure real uploads with the provider's counter, per language, and watch actual usage

coldCase.model: He estimated from the wrong sample. My cards were short and all in Dutch and English, and his users send Greek, Polish and Vietnamese, long lists of names and dates, all of which can split into more tokens than a rule of thumb or my averages expect. His page of instructions is input tokens on every single upload, and the English translations coming back are output tokens, billed at the higher price. He should sample real uploads from each language his users write in, count them with the provider's token counter for the model he uses, price input and output separately, budget by the expected mix of languages, cut the instructions to what's needed, and watch the usage the service reports against his estimate every week.

sources.title: Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units, ACL 2016, pages 1715 to 1725: byte pair encoding as a compression technique (Gage, 1994) adapted to word segmentation; start from characters, count all symbol pairs, replace the most frequent pair with a new symbol; final vocabulary size is the initial vocabulary plus the number of merge operations, the only hyperparameter; no pairs across word boundaries; among 100 rare German tokens, 56 compounds and 21 names

OpenAI, tiktoken on GitHub: a fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI's models; reversible and lossless; works on arbitrary text; on average each token corresponds to about 4 bytes; encoding split into encod and ing

OpenAI Help Center, What are tokens and how to count them (rough estimates for English text: 1 token is approximately 4 characters, or three-quarters of a word, and 100 tokens approximately 75 words; estimates, not exact counts; other languages differ, and counts depend on the model, its encoding and the language; input and output tokens tracked separately and can have different prices)

Anthropic, Pricing (Claude Platform docs): prices per million tokens (MTok) for input and output; output five times input on every listed model when checked in October 2026; the worked example 50,000 x $5 / 1,000,000 = $0.25 and 15,000 x $25 / 1,000,000 = $0.375; Claude 4.7 and later use a newer tokenizer with approximately 30% more tokens for the same text
Anthropic, Token counting (Claude Platform docs): count a message's tokens before sending; the count is an estimate; free to use within rate limits; recount prompts against the model you plan to use

Petrov, La Malfa, Torr and Bibi, Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages, NeurIPS 2023: the same text in different languages can differ in tokenization length up to 15 times; gaps persist for multilingual tokenizers; over 4 times for character-level and byte-level models; unfair cost, latency and context
